topics.title: The financial system
topics.detail: A financial system is the network that moves money from people or organisations with surplus funds to those who need funds.
topics.simple: Think of it as the economy's money-connection system: savers, borrowers, markets, institutions and regulators all connect through it.
topics.example: A household saves money in a bank. The bank lends to a business that needs funds to buy equipment. The system connects the saver and borrower.
points: It includes financial markets, institutions, instruments and services, with regulators supervising the system.
topics.key: Markets enable issue and trading; institutions collect, lend, invest and insure; instruments are products such as shares and bonds; regulators supervise participants.

topics.detail: Tracking error measures how closely an index fund follows its benchmark.
topics.simple: It measures how much the fund's return differs from the index over time.
topics.example: If the index returns 2% and the fund returns 1.8%, the difference for that period is −0.2 percentage points.

topics.title: Forward contracts
topics.detail: A forward contract is a customised, bilateral agreement between two parties to buy or sell an agreed quantity and quality of an underlying asset at a price fixed today, with settlement on a specified future date. The lecture describes forwards as over-the-counter (OTC): the parties negotiate directly rather than trading a standardised exchange contract.
topics.simple: Two parties privately lock in a price today for a transaction that will happen later. Both sides are committed to the agreed terms.
topics.example: The lecture's gold example: on 9 December 2014, a jeweller agrees to buy 15 kg of 999-purity gold from a dealer after three months at ₹2,450 per gram. The agreed amount is ₹3.675 crore. If the market price at settlement is ₹2,700/g, the jeweller benefits because the contract price is lower. If it is ₹2,050/g, the jeweller is still bound to pay ₹2,450/g.
points: Forward contracts are private OTC agreements and can be customised for quantity, quality, price and delivery date.
The buyer takes a long position and agrees to buy; the seller takes a short position and agrees to sell.
Both parties are obligated to complete the contract at the agreed price and date; unlike an option, neither side simply has a right to walk away.
Scenario 1 in the slides: gold rises from ₹2,450/g to ₹2,700/g. The jeweller saves approximately ₹38 lakh compared with buying at the new market price; the dealer bears the corresponding loss.

Scenario 2: gold falls to ₹2,050/g. The jeweller must still buy at ₹2,450/g. The slide states a loss of about ₹59.5 lakh and a matching dealer gain. The displayed deal values (₹3.675 crore and ₹3.075 crore) imply ₹60 lakh, so treat ₹59.5 lakh as the slide's stated rounded figure.
Scenario 3: if the market price remains at the original level, neither party gains from the price movement.

Key risks highlighted: liquidity risk (finding an opposite counterparty can be difficult), counterparty/default risk, regulatory risk (the lecture notes the bilateral OTC structure), and rigidity (the contract can be difficult to exit early).

topics.title: Futures contracts
topics.detail: A futures contract is a standardised agreement traded on an exchange to buy or sell an underlying asset at a predetermined price for a specified expiry. The exchange standardises key terms such as lot size and expiry, and the clearing system supports settlement.
topics.simple: A forward-like agreement, but standardised and exchange-traded. You can usually exit by taking the opposite position instead of waiting for expiry.
topics.example: The lecture gives an Infosys illustration: buy futures at ₹1,651 and sell at ₹1,653. With a lot size of 250, the gross gain is (₹1,653 − ₹1,651) × 250 = ₹500, before transaction costs.
points: Lot size is the minimum quantity specified in the futures contract; expiry is the last date up to which the contract can be held.
Contract value = Futures price × Lot size.
To enter a futures position, a trader deposits margin, a fraction of the full contract value. This creates leverage.
Futures are tradable before expiry: an investor can close the position with an opposite trade, even intraday, subject to market liquidity and costs.
The lecture states that equity index futures in India are cash-settled; the slide contrasts this with physical delivery examples in other markets.
Futures have a linear payoff: for a long, payoff = settlement/expiry futures price − original futures price; for a short, reverse the subtraction.
Long futures generally benefit when the futures price rises; short futures generally benefit when it falls.
The lecture describes futures as regulated by SEBI and contrasts their exchange framework with OTC forwards.
Leverage magnifies both gains and losses. A small price movement can have a large effect relative to the margin deposited.

The lecture's Nifty Index Futures section describes the index as a basket of 50 stocks and explains that the futures contract derives its value from the Nifty spot index. The lot-size figure of 75 and quoted prices are from the slide snapshot and should be treated as historical classroom data, not today's contract specification.

Open interest (OI) is the number of outstanding contracts that have not yet been closed or expired. Every open contract has one long and one short, so the number of longs equals the number of shorts and equals OI.
New long + new short creates a new contract and increases OI. An old long and old short closing together reduces OI. When one participant exits and another enters (a transfer), OI remains unchanged.
topics.key: Do not confuse contract value with margin. Contract value is the full exposure; margin is the amount deposited to support the position. The examples in the slides are historical illustrations, not current lot-size or margin advice.

points: Contract value = futures price × lot size.

topics.title: Mark-to-market
topics.detail: Mark-to-market (MTM) is the daily settlement of gains and losses on a futures position using the change in the futures closing price. The lecture's tables track daily contract value, daily gain/loss, margin balance and any deposit or withdrawal needed to restore the required margin level.
topics.simple: At the end of each trading day, the exchange works out how much your futures position gained or lost and adjusts your margin balance.
topics.example: For a long position of 200 units, a move in futures closing price from ₹600 to ₹550 produces daily MTM = (₹550 − ₹600) × 200 = −₹10,000. The lecture's table starts with ₹30,000 initial margin and ₹20,000 minimum margin.
points: For a long position: daily MTM = (today's closing futures price − previous day's closing/reference price) × quantity.
For a short position, reverse the price difference: (previous reference price − today's closing price) × quantity.
A positive MTM is a gain credited to the position; a negative MTM is a loss debited from it.
After MTM, compare the margin balance with the initial and minimum margin thresholds shown in the question.
In the 200-unit classroom table, the initial margin is ₹30,000 and minimum margin is ₹20,000. A fall from ₹600 to ₹550 creates a ₹10,000 loss and reduces the balance to ₹20,000.
A second Nifty illustration uses 750 units and initial margin of approximately ₹14,90,303; the slide's summary reports total MTM loss of ₹4,39,200 across the shown dates.
The table's sign convention says a negative amount in the withdrawal/deposit column means the investor deposits money; a positive amount means a withdrawal.
topics.key: Keep the price movement, quantity and position direction clear. A common error is to use the long formula for a short position or to calculate the margin adjustment before updating the MTM balance.
topics.classNotes: Class note: Mark-to-market settles the daily gain or loss on an open futures position. A long position gains when the settlement price rises and loses when it falls; a short position behaves in the opposite way. Margin may need replenishment after adverse daily movements.

topics.title: Cost of carry and fair futures price
topics.detail: Cost of carry explains the relationship between an underlying asset's spot price and its fair futures price. The lecture starts with financing/carrying costs and then adjusts for cash inflows such as dividends on shares or interest on bonds received during the holding period.
topics.simple: Holding an asset until the futures expiry can cost money, but it may also generate income. The fair futures price reflects both.
topics.example: The lecture's Nifty illustration uses spot value 1,150, financing cost 11% p.a., dividend yield 1% p.a. and one month to expiry: F = 1,150 × [1 + (11% − 1%)]^(1/12), approximately 1,159.
points: Spot price is the current market price of the underlying in the cash/spot market; futures price is the price of the futures contract.
Basis is the difference between the current futures price and current spot price (the slide labels it as futures price minus spot price).
Cost of carry includes the financing/carrying cost of holding the underlying.
For assets that generate income during the holding period, such as dividends or bond interest, the lecture adjusts the fair futures price downward for those inflows.
Slide formula: Fair price = Spot price + Cost of carry − Inflows.

Modified formula shown: F = S(1 + r − q)^T, where F is fair futures price, S is spot price, r is cost of carry/financing rate, q is expected holding-period return/income yield, and T is time in years.

The lecture lists assumptions such as abundant availability, no seasonal supply constraint, ease of maintaining/holding the asset, short-selling feasibility, no transaction costs, no taxes and no margin requirements. It notes that if these assumptions fail, adjustments may be needed.
topics.key: Use consistent time units: if the annual rate is given and expiry is one month away, express T as 1/12 year. Include income yield when the underlying pays dividends or interest.

topics.title: Options: calls and puts
topics.detail: An option is a derivative that gives its buyer a right, but not an obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specified strike price. The option seller/writer receives the premium and takes on the corresponding obligation if the buyer exercises.
topics.simple: The buyer pays for a choice. A call is the right to buy; a put is the right to sell. The seller receives the premium and must honour the contract if exercised.

Strike price is the exercise price fixed in the contract; premium is the option price paid by the buyer and received by the seller.
Premium and strike are not the same. The slide Q&A explicitly distinguishes them.
An out-of-the-money put can still have a premium because time value and volatility can contribute to the option's price.

LTP (last traded price) is the price of the most recent trade; it is not necessarily the price at which your own order will execute. A buyer crossing the spread may pay the ask; a limit order may execute at a different price.

topics.key: Do not call the premium the strike price. Strike = agreed exercise price; premium = market price paid/received for the option.

topics.title: Option payoff and moneyness
topics.detail: At expiry, option payoff is the value obtained from exercising the option, if exercise is favourable. Net profit/loss is different because it also includes the premium paid by the buyer or received by the seller.
topics.simple: First calculate what the option is worth at expiry. Then subtract the premium you paid (or account for the premium you received if you sold it).
topics.example: Long call net P/L = max(S − K, 0) − premium. Long put net P/L = max(K − S, 0) − premium. S is expiry market price and K is strike price.
points: A call is in-the-money (ITM) when S > K; a put is ITM when S < K.
At-the-money (ATM) means market price and strike are equal or very close, subject to the convention used.
An option is out-of-the-money (OTM) when immediate exercise would not be beneficial.
Intrinsic value is the immediate exercise value; time value is the part of the premium above intrinsic value.
Time value = premium − intrinsic value.
For a long call, expiry payoff = max(S − K, 0); net P/L = payoff − premium paid.
For a long put, expiry payoff = max(K − S, 0); net P/L = payoff − premium paid.
The buyer's maximum loss is the premium paid, while the seller's risk depends on the option position and underlying movement.
topics.key: Never confuse payoff with net P/L. A payoff calculation alone does not include the premium.
topics.classNotes: Class note: Intrinsic value is the immediate exercise value; time value is the portion of premium above intrinsic value. A call is in-the-money when market price is above strike; a put is in-the-money when market price is below strike. topics.example: A bull call spread buys a call at a lower strike and sells a call at a higher strike with the same expiry. The premium received on the short call reduces the initial cost, but the upside is capped.

topics.detail: A covered call combines ownership of the underlying shares with the sale (writing) of a call option on those shares. The premium received provides income and cushions a small fall, but the short call limits gains above its strike.
topics.simple: You already own the shares, and you sell someone else the right to buy them from you at the strike. You collect a premium, but you may have to sell the shares at that strike.
topics.example: Class example: 500 Reliance shares at ₹2,400; short call strike ₹2,500; premium ₹45. Break-even ₹2,355; maximum gain ₹145 per share under the example's one-to-one assumption.
points: Position = long shares + short call.

Short-call P/L includes the premium received and the call obligation if S exceeds the strike.
Break-even for the combined position = share purchase price − call premium received, under the one-share/one-option-unit assumption.
The maximum gain is capped once the share price rises above the call strike; the premium offers only a limited cushion against a share-price fall.
topics.key: The word covered refers to already owning the underlying shares against the call written. Always check the share/option lot ratio before applying a per-share example.
topics.classNotes: Class note: A covered call is used when the investor already owns the underlying and sells a call to collect premium. The premium cushions a limited fall, but upside is capped above the strike because the short call may be exercised.

theory.question: Explain The financial system in your own words.
theory.modelAnswer: A financial system is the network that moves money from people or organisations with surplus funds to those who need funds. Think of it as the economy's money-connection system: savers, borrowers, markets, institutions and regulators all connect through it. A household saves money in a bank. The bank lends to a business that needs funds to buy equipment. The system connects the saver and borrower. It includes financial markets, institutions, instruments and services, with regulators supervising the system. Markets enable issue and trading; institutions collect, lend, invest and insure; instruments are products such as shares and bonds; regulators supervise participants.
theory.gradingNote: Similar wording is accepted. Include the key ideas, not necessarily the exact sentences.

theory.question: Explain Financial markets and their functions in your own words.
theory.modelAnswer: Financial markets are systems where financial assets are created, issued and traded. A market connects buyers and sellers and helps establish a price for financial products. An investor sells listed shares to another investor through the secondary market.
